title: Teach Us to Count Our Days
sum: Book IV of the Psalter opens with the only psalm credited to Moses. It sets the eternal God, who was there before the mountains were born, against human beings who return to powder, grow like grass and wither by evening, and whose seventy or eighty years pass "like a low moan" (90:9). Their brief lives lie under God's anger, and their hidden guilt lies open in the light of his face.

Then the prayer turns. Moses asks for wisdom to count the days, for God to "turn back" and change his mind, as at Sinai (Exodus 32:12), and for loyal love at daybreak, so that the years of trouble are matched by years of gladness. The psalm ends by asking that the work of human hands, which cannot outlast its makers, be given firm footing by God. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 89.
readings: Read as Moses' prayer in the wilderness

The Targum heads it "when the people, the house of Israel, sinned in the wilderness." Read this way, the psalm is Moses watching a generation die over forty years (Numbers 14:29–35) and praying for their children (90:16).
Read as an answer to Psalm 89

At the head of Book IV, right after the lament over David's fallen throne, the psalm goes back to the time before kings and temple, when God himself was Israel's home (90:1). Many scholars read Book IV as the exiles' answer: the LORD reigns even without a king.
Read as a meditation on every human life
Jews and Christians have prayed it at funerals and at the turning of the year, as a mirror for anyone who wants to live wisely in a short life.

views.H: Traditional readers take the title at face value: Moses, "the man of God," prayed it near the end of the wilderness years, perhaps after the deaths of Miriam and Aaron. Its echoes of Deuteronomy 32–33 fit his voice.
views.C: Most critical scholars date the psalm to the time after the exile, from its wisdom tone and late language, and read the title as the editors' way of letting Moses speak at the head of Book IV. They note its close ties to Psalm 91 ("home," 90:1; 91:9) and to Deuteronomy 32.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 89. It is read at funerals in Anglican, Lutheran and other churches (the Book of Common Prayer of 1662 sets it in the burial service) and on New Year's Eve; Isaac Watts' "O God, Our Help in Ages Past" (1719) is a paraphrase of it. In the synagogue it is part of the Sabbath and festival morning psalms, and 90:17 is said with Psalm 91 at the close of the Sabbath.
views.J: The Midrash on Psalms and Rashi credit Psalms 90–100 to Moses, eleven psalms for the eleven tribes he blessed in Deuteronomy 33. The Talmud names Moses among the elders whose words are in the Psalter (Bava Batra 14b–15a). The Mishnah's ages of life (Avot 5:21) draw on 90:10.
views.X: Second Peter 3:8 takes up 90:4 to explain the delay of Christ's return. Luther lectured on the psalm in 1534–1535 and read it as Moses' sermon of the law, which shows that death is the wages of sin so that people will flee to God's mercy. Augustine read the "turning back" of 90:13 as the hope of conversion.

deep.b: The psalm works by contrast. On one side stands God: "from the ages past to the ages to come, you are God" (90:2), for whom a thousand years are a night watch (90:4). On the other stand human beings: powder, sleep, grass, a moan, a short flight (90:3–10). The psalm does not say that the shortness of life is merely natural. It ties it to God's anger at sin (90:7–9), as Genesis 3:19 does. Yet it does not end in despair. The same God who is eternal is asked to be the home of his people in every generation (90:1), to have pity (90:13), to fill their mornings with loyal love (90:14) and to make their work last (90:17). Eternity is not only the measure that shames human time; it is also the only ground on which a short human life can be built.

For this part the writer checked these directly: the Hebrew (Leningrad Codex); the Greek in Swete's edition of Codex Vaticanus, with his apparatus for Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, the Verona Psalter and others; Jerome's Gallican Psalter and his Psalter from the Hebrew; the Targum in Aramaic (with an English translation for 90–92); Rashi, Radak and the Midrash on Psalms; Mishnah Tamid 7:4 and Bavli Rosh Hashanah 31a. Rahlfs' critical text was not checked directly. Qumran readings (4QPs-b, -k, -m, 11QPs-a, 11Q11), the Syriac, and other Hebrew manuscripts are given as reported by their editors and commentators.

echoes: Deuteronomy 33:1; Deuteronomy 32:18; Deuteronomy 32:36; Exodus 32:12–14; Genesis 3:19; Numbers 14:29–35; Isaiah 40:6–8; 2 Peter 3:8; James 4:14; Psalm 39:4–6; Psalm 103:14–16
links: O God, Our Help in Ages Past
O God, Our Help in Ages Past

settings.what: A community lament and prayer for wisdom
settings.by: Moses, "the man of God," according to the title, speaking for the people ("us," "our")
settings.when: On the title's view, during the wilderness years, as the generation that left Egypt died out. On most scholars' view, after the exile, when Israel had lost its king and temple and lived under foreign rule.
settings.why: To set the shortness and guilt of human life honestly before the eternal God, and to ask him to turn, to have pity, and to give back years of gladness for years of trouble. It teaches the people to pray from inside God's anger, not to hide from it.
settings.readers: For the exiles and those who came back, the psalm placed at the head of Book IV said that before there was a king in Jerusalem, God was Israel's home, and he could be so again.
views: The title and Jewish and Christian tradition (Rashi, Luther).
Most critical scholars (Tate, Hossfeld and Zenger), reading the title as an editorial link to Moses.

title: Under His Wings
sum: Psalm 91 is the Bible's great song of protection. Whoever lives in the hiding place of the Most High will be safe from the bird-catcher's trap, from plague and scourge, from terrors of the night and arrows of the day. Thousands may fall nearby; harm will not touch the one who trusts. God will give his angels orders to guard him, and he will tread on lion and serpent.

The voices shift: someone confesses trust (91:2, 9), someone promises safety (91:3–13), and at the end God himself speaks seven promises over the one who loves him (91:14–16). The devil quotes this psalm to Jesus in the temptation story. Jews and Christians have long prayed it at night, in danger and at funerals. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 90.
readings: Read as a temple liturgy
Many scholars think a worshiper, a priest and finally a word from God speak in turn, perhaps when someone came to the temple seeking shelter.
Read as a prayer against evil powers

The Greek and the Targum speak of demons in 91:5–6, and a Qumran scroll of songs for driving out demons ends with this psalm. In Jewish and Christian practice it has been prayed for protection against every evil.
Read as the psalm of the Son
The temptation story makes it a test of Jesus: will he use God's promises to force God's hand? Christian readers have heard 91:14–16 as the Father's promise to the Son, kept in the resurrection.

views.H: The Hebrew has no title; the Greek and the Qumran scroll 11Q11 call it David's. Rabbinic tradition counted it among Moses' psalms (90–100). The Targum makes it a dialogue between David, Solomon and God.
views.C: Scholars read it as a psalm of trust from the temple, with oracle-like promises, perhaps from the late monarchy or after the exile. They compare ancient protective texts and amulets against plague and demons, and note its many links with Psalm 90.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 90. It is the psalm of Compline, the church's night prayer, in the Rule of Benedict and the Roman and Anglican traditions, and it is read on the first Sunday of Lent with the temptation Gospel. In the synagogue it is said at bedtime, at the close of the Sabbath and at funerals.
views.J: The Talmud calls it a "song against afflictions" (Shevuot 15b). The Targum names the night terror as demons and the noonday scourge as "the band of demons that attacks at noon." Rashi says Moses is urging people to shelter under the wings of the Shekhinah.
views.X: Matthew 4:6 and Luke 4:10–11 put 91:11–12 in the devil's mouth. Augustine, Cassiodorus and others read the psalm as Christ's: he is the one who trusted the Father to the end and was raised. Luther and Calvin taught that its promises are true even when believers suffer, because nothing touches them outside God's care.

deep.h: Psalm 91 at Qumran and the temptation
deep.b: Two very different uses of Psalm 91 come from the time of Jesus. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, 11Q11 (the "Apocryphal Psalms") gathers songs for driving out demons, some credited to David and Solomon, and ends with a form of Psalm 91 headed "Of David." So the psalm was already being used as a protective prayer, a shield against evil spirits. In the Gospels the devil uses the same psalm as a weapon: he takes Jesus to the pinnacle of the temple and invites him to jump, quoting 91:11–12 (Matthew 4:5–7; Luke 4:9–12). Jesus answers from Deuteronomy 6:16, "Do not put the LORD your God to the test," the verse that recalls Massah (Psalm 95:8). The contrast teaches how the psalm works: its promises are given to the one who "lives in the hiding place of the Most High" (91:1), who trusts and calls on God, not to someone who tries to make God prove himself.

echoes: Deuteronomy 32:11; Ruth 2:12; Matthew 4:5–7; Luke 4:9–12; Luke 10:19; Matthew 23:37; Exodus 12:23; Habakkuk 3:5; Genesis 3:15; Romans 16:20; Hebrews 1:14

traditions.q: Does every person have a guardian angel?
views: Yes: "Beside each believer stands an angel as protector and shepherd leading him to life" (Catechism 336, quoting Basil), resting on 91:11 and Matthew 18:10; the Church keeps a feast of the Guardian Angels.
Yes: each Christian receives a guardian angel at baptism, invoked in daily prayers and the evening prayers of the prayer book.
Angels watch over God's people, but Scripture does not clearly teach that each person has one assigned angel. Calvin wrote that he dared not affirm it (Institutes 1.14.7).
Luther and the catechisms speak gladly of God's "holy angel" guarding the believer (the Morning and Evening Prayers of the Small Catechism) without making a doctrine of one angel for each person.

settings.what: A psalm of trust with promises and a closing word from God
settings.by: Voices that change: a worshiper confessing trust (91:2, 9a), a speaker promising protection (91:3–13), and God himself (91:14–16)
settings.to: A person seeking God's protection ("you"), and God (91:2, 9)
settings.when: Perhaps when someone came to the temple for shelter in danger or illness; the psalm itself names no occasion.
settings.why: To give a person in danger words of trust and the assurance of God's care, ending with God's own promise to rescue, answer and honor the one who loves him.
settings.readers: For later Israel, at home and in exile, it became a prayer against plague, night terrors and evil powers, said at night and over the dead.

title: A Song for the Sabbath
sum: Psalm 92 is the only psalm the Hebrew assigns to a day: the Sabbath. It begins with the goodness of thanking the LORD morning and night, on harp and lyre, for the works of his hands. The stupid cannot see what the singer sees: the wicked spring up like grass only to be cut down, while the LORD stays on high forever.

The singer has been made strong like a wild ox and refreshed with oil. The righteous will grow like palm and cedar, planted in the temple courts, still fruitful in old age, and their flourishing shows that the LORD is straight, a rock with no wrong in him (92:15, echoing Deuteronomy 32:4). In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 91.
readings: Read as a Sabbath hymn
Sung by the Levites at the Sabbath offerings, the psalm praises God for his works and rests in his justice.
Read as a wisdom psalm
Like Psalms 1, 37 and 73, it answers the question of why the wicked thrive, using the two plants: grass and trees.
Read as a song of the age to come
The Mishnah calls it a song for the day that will be all Sabbath, when the wicked are gone and the righteous flourish forever.

views.H: The Hebrew title gives no author; the Targum says the first man, Adam, sang it on the first Sabbath. Rabbinic tradition counted it among Moses' psalms.
views.C: Scholars classify it as a thanksgiving hymn with strong wisdom themes, probably for temple use. They note the Ugaritic-style three-part line in 92:9 and the link to Deuteronomy 32:4 in 92:15.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 91. In the synagogue it closes Kabbalat Shabbat on Friday evening and is sung on Sabbath morning. In the Roman Liturgy of the Hours it is used at Saturday morning prayer, and many Christians sing it on the Lord's Day.
views.J: The Mishnah lists it as the Levites' Sabbath psalm (Tamid 7:4). The Targum and the Midrash connect it to Adam's repentance on the first Sabbath. Rashi says it speaks of the world to come.
views.X: Christian readers have heard 92:12–14 of the righteous rooted in Christ and the church, bearing fruit (John 15:5). Augustine read the grass and the cedar as the passing glory of the wicked and the lasting life of the faithful.

deep.h: The daily psalms of the temple
deep.b: The Mishnah lists a psalm for each day, sung by the Levites at the morning offering: Sunday, Psalm 24; Monday, 48; Tuesday, 82; Wednesday, 94; Thursday, 81; Friday, 93; Sabbath, 92 (Tamid 7:4). The Talmud explains each from the days of creation: on the fourth day God made the sun and moon, and he will punish those who worship them (Psalm 94); on the sixth he finished his work and reigned (Psalm 93) (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 31a). The Greek Psalter's titles for Psalms 24, 48, 93 and 94 name the same days, so the custom goes back at least to the centuries before Christ. Of the seven, only Psalm 92 has its day in the Hebrew title. Synagogues still recite the psalm of the day at the end of the morning service.
deep.refs: 92:0; Psalm 24:1; Psalm 48:1; Psalm 82:1; Psalm 94:1; Psalm 81:1; Psalm 93:1; Genesis 1:14–19; Genesis 2:1–3

echoes: Genesis 2:1–3; Deuteronomy 32:4; Psalm 1:3–4; Psalm 37:1–2; Psalm 52:8; Jeremiah 17:7–8; 1 Kings 6:29; Isaiah 58:13–14; Hebrews 4:9; Luke 1:69

settings.by: A singer speaking for himself ("me," "my horn"), probably a Levite or a worshiper who has been rescued
settings.to: The LORD (92:1–5, 8–10) and the gathered worshipers (92:6–7, 12–15)
settings.when: At the Sabbath offerings in the temple, according to the title and the Mishnah
settings.why: To praise God for his works and for his justice, and to teach that the wicked's thriving is short while the righteous, rooted in God's house, last. It turns the Sabbath rest into confident praise.
settings.readers: After the exile the Sabbath became one of the marks of Jewish identity (Nehemiah 13:15–22). The psalm gave it a song of trust in God's justice.

title: The LORD Is King
sum: Psalm 93 is the first of the psalms of the LORD's kingship (93–99), and one of three that open with the cry "The LORD is King!" (93, 97, 99). In five verses it pictures the LORD dressed in majesty and strength like a king in his robe and belt. Because he reigns, the world stands firm and will not totter. His throne has stood from the start.

Then the rivers raise their voices, three times, in pounding waves. But the LORD on high is greater than the roar of the vast waters and the breakers of the sea. The psalm ends quietly: his decrees can be trusted, and holiness fits his house forever. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 92.
readings: Read as the King above chaos
The sea and rivers are the old picture of chaos. The psalm says they roar, but they cannot shake the world the LORD has set firm.
Read as a festival song
Mowinckel and others read it as part of a yearly celebration of the LORD's enthronement, perhaps at the autumn festival.
Read as the answer of Book IV
After Psalm 89's fallen throne of David, Psalm 93 announces a throne that has never fallen.

views.H: The Hebrew has no title; the Greek gives it to David and to "the day before the Sabbath." Rabbinic tradition counted it among Moses' psalms.
views.C: Many scholars think it is one of the oldest psalms, close to Canaanite poetry about Baal's kingship and his victory over Sea and River. They debate whether "is King" or "has become King" is meant (see 93:1).
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 92. It was the Levites' psalm for Friday (Tamid 7:4) and still is in the synagogue; it follows Psalm 92 in the Friday evening service. In the church it opened Sunday Lauds in the Roman Breviary before 1911, and the current Roman lectionary sings it on the feast of Christ the King in Year B.
views.J: The Talmud links it to the sixth day of creation, when God finished his work and reigned over all he made (Rosh Hashanah 31a). Radak reads 93:5 as the hope that the temple will never be destroyed again.
views.X: Christians have read the King clothed in majesty as the risen Christ. Revelation's songs of God's reign use the image of the roar of many waters (Revelation 19:6).

deep.h: The psalms of the LORD's kingship (93–100)
deep.b:
Psalms 93 and 95 to 99 are often called the "enthronement psalms" or "kingship of the LORD" psalms. Three begin with YHWH malakh, "The LORD is King!" (93:1; 97:1; 99:1), and the cry is the center of 96:10. They praise God as Creator (93:1; 95:4–5; 96:5, 10), as King over the gods (95:3; 96:4; 97:7, 9), as Judge who is coming to set the earth right (96:13; 98:9), and as the holy God of Zion who spoke to Moses, Aaron and Samuel (99:6–7). Psalm 94, a cry for justice, sits among them because the King is the one who judges, and Psalm 100 ends the group with all the earth entering his gates.

How these psalms were first used is debated. Sigmund Mowinckel argued for a yearly festival of the LORD's enthronement, at the autumn New Year, when the ark was carried up to the temple and God was hailed as King again. Hans-Joachim Kraus proposed a festival of Zion and the ark instead. Many recent scholars, such as Gerald Wilson and David Howard, read the group above all as the editors' answer to the crisis of Psalm 89: Israel's kings have failed, but the LORD reigns. Jewish tradition kept them together in the Friday evening service, and the church in its morning prayer.

echoes: Exodus 15:18; 1 Chronicles 16:30–31; Psalm 29:3–10; Psalm 89:9–10; Psalm 104:1–5; Isaiah 51:9–10; Revelation 19:6; Revelation 1:15

settings.what: A hymn proclaiming the LORD as King
settings.by: A temple singer or the congregation
settings.to: The worshipers (93:1), then the LORD himself (93:2–5)
settings.when: In temple worship; many scholars think at a festival celebrating God's kingship, perhaps in autumn. The Levites later sang it every Friday.
settings.why: To proclaim that the LORD rules over the world and over every chaotic power, so that worshipers can trust the stability of his creation, his decrees and his house.
settings.readers: For Jews under Persian, Greek and Roman rule, it said that the true throne was not in Susa, Alexandria or Rome.
views: A festival of Zion and the ark

title: God Who Takes Vengeance
sum: Psalm 94 is a cry for justice. It calls on the God who takes vengeance to shine out and on the Judge of the earth to rise and pay back the proud. In Israel itself, arrogant people crush God's people, kill widows, foreigners and orphans, and say that the LORD does not see.

The singer turns on them: the one who planted the ear and shaped the eye sees and hears. Happy is the one God trains through his law, for the LORD will not let go of his people. The singer tells how God held him up when his foot slipped and comforted him when his thoughts piled up. A throne that makes misery into law can never be God's partner, and God will turn its wrongdoing back on it. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 93.
readings: Read as a protest against corrupt rulers
Most scholars hear oppression from inside Judah: judges and officials who use the law to destroy the weak (94:20–21).
Read as a wisdom psalm
The middle section (94:8–15) teaches like Proverbs: God sees, disciplines and will not abandon his people.
Read as a prayer of every victim
Jews and Christians have prayed it under persecution, handing vengeance over to God rather than taking it themselves.

views.H: The Hebrew has no title; the Greek reads "A psalm of David, for the fourth day of the week." Rabbinic tradition counted it among Moses' psalms.
views.C: Scholars call it a mixed form: a community lament (94:1–7), a wisdom instruction (94:8–15) and an individual thanksgiving (94:16–23). Most date it after the exile. Its place among the kingship psalms ties the King to justice.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 93. It was the Levites' psalm for Wednesday (Tamid 7:4) and still is in the synagogue. The Liturgy of the Hours keeps it, but it is rarely read at Sunday worship.
views.J: The Talmud explains the Wednesday use from the fourth day of creation, when God made sun and moon: he will punish those who worship them (Rosh Hashanah 31a). Rashi reads 94:9 as God hearing the cry of his afflicted people.
views.X: Paul quotes 94:11 in 1 Corinthians 3:20 and echoes 94:14 in Romans 11:1–2. Christian teachers have read the call for vengeance alongside Romans 12:19: vengeance belongs to God, and so believers do not take it themselves.

echoes: Deuteronomy 32:35; Deuteronomy 32:43; Genesis 18:25; Exodus 22:21–24; Isaiah 10:1–2; Proverbs 3:11–12; 1 Corinthians 3:20; Romans 11:1–2; Romans 12:19; Hebrews 12:5–11

settings.what: A lament and cry for justice, with teaching and testimony
settings.by: A singer speaking for the oppressed community ("your people," 94:5) and for himself ("me," 94:16–19)
settings.to: God (94:1–7, 12, 18–20), the arrogant oppressors among the people (94:8–11), and anyone listening
settings.when: When powerful people in Israel used their position and even the law to crush the weak; most scholars think after the exile.
settings.why: To bring the injustice to the Judge of the earth, to warn the oppressors that God sees, to teach that God's discipline and law steady the faithful, and to give victims words of trust instead of revenge.
settings.readers: For Jews of the Second Temple period, often ruled by corrupt officials and foreign powers, the psalm promised that the LORD would not abandon his inheritance (94:14).

title: Today, If You Would Only Listen
sum: Psalm 95 begins as a joyful call to worship: come, shout to the rock that saves us, for the LORD is a great King over all the gods, who holds the depths and the heights and made the sea and the dry ground. Come in, bow low and kneel before the one who made us, for we are the flock he pastures.

Then the tone changes. "Today, if you would only listen to his voice!" God himself speaks a warning: do not harden your hearts as your ancestors did at Meribah and Massah, when they put him on trial. For forty years he was sick of that generation and swore they would never enter his rest. Hebrews 3–4 builds a whole sermon on these verses. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 94.
readings: Read as a temple entrance liturgy
The people approach the temple in praise (95:1–7a), and a priest or prophet speaks God's warning as they enter (95:7b–11).
Read as the church's daily call
As the Venite, it opens Christian daily prayer: each day begins with praise and the warning not to harden one's heart.
Read through Hebrews
Hebrews hears "Today" as still open and "my rest" as God's own Sabbath rest, which believers in Christ can still enter.

views.H: The Hebrew has no title; the Greek calls it "a praise of a song, of David," and Hebrews 4:7 says God spoke "through David." Rabbinic tradition counted it among Moses' psalms.
views.C: Scholars see two parts, a hymn and a prophetic warning, and many think they were joined for a festival, perhaps the autumn feast when the covenant was renewed. The warning draws on Exodus 17, Numbers 14 and 20, and Deuteronomy 1.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 94. The Invitatory psalm of the Liturgy of the Hours and the Rule of Benedict; the Venite of the Book of Common Prayer. In the synagogue it opens Kabbalat Shabbat on Friday evening.
views.J: Radak reads the call "Come" as Israel urging one another in the days of the Messiah. Rashi takes "today" as "in this world." The Talmud's Messiah answers Rabbi Joshua ben Levi "Today", meaning today if you listen (Sanhedrin 98a). The Mishnah counts the ten times Israel tested God in the wilderness (Avot 5:4).
views.X: Hebrews 3:7–4:11 quotes 95:7–11 from the Greek and argues that the promised rest remains, a Sabbath rest for God's people (Hebrews 4:9). Paul uses the wilderness testing as a warning in 1 Corinthians 10:1–13.

deep.b:
Hebrews quotes Psalm 95:7–11 in full (Hebrews 3:7–11) and then preaches on three words. "Today": as long as it is called today, the call to listen still stands, so the readers must encourage one another every day (Hebrews 3:13). "Hearts": the wilderness generation heard God's voice, saw his works, and still did not believe; their bodies fell in the wilderness (Hebrews 3:16–19). "My rest": God's rest is older than Canaan, because God rested on the seventh day (Hebrews 4:4, quoting Genesis 2:2). If Joshua had given Israel the true rest, God would not still say "Today" through David long afterward (Hebrews 4:7–8). So "a Sabbath rest is still waiting for God's people" (Hebrews 4:9), and whoever enters it rests from his works as God did from his.

Hebrews reads the Greek text, with "rebellion" and "testing" in place of Meribah and Massah, and joins "forty years" to the line before (see 95:10). The psalm itself already looked beyond the land: it was sung by Israelites who lived in the land, and still warned them that they could miss God's rest.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Psalm 95 as the hinge between the wilderness and the King
deep.b: This is my own suggestion. Psalms 90 to 95 move from Moses' wilderness (Psalm 90, a generation dying under God's anger) to the warning about the wilderness (95:8–11). In between stand the promises of shelter (91), the Sabbath song (92), and the King who reigns over the sea (93). I read Psalm 95 as the hinge of Book IV: it gathers the kingship of 93 ("a great King," 95:3) and the Sabbath theme of 92 ("rest," 95:11) and then asks the exiles, who had lost the land, the old question: will you listen today? The psalms that follow (96–100) invite all nations into the worship that Israel's ancestors refused. Gerald Wilson, Erich Zenger and David Howard have argued for close links among these psalms; my addition is only to read "rest" in 95:11 as deliberately answering the Sabbath of Psalm 92, as Hebrews 4 would later do.

echoes: Exodus 17:1–7; Numbers 14:20–35; Numbers 20:1–13; Deuteronomy 1:34–35; Deuteronomy 6:16; Deuteronomy 12:9; Hebrews 3:7–4:11; 1 Corinthians 10:1–13; Psalm 81:7–13; Psalm 100:3

traditions.q: Hebrews 4:9 says "a Sabbath rest remains." Must Christians keep a weekly Sabbath?
views: Yes: the seventh-day Sabbath, Saturday, remains binding as part of the Ten Commandments and a sign of creation and redemption; Hebrews 4:9's "Sabbath rest" (sabbatismos) is read as confirming it.
Yes, on the Lord's Day: from Christ's resurrection the Sabbath moved to the first day of the week, to be kept holy by rest and worship (Westminster Confession 21.7–8).
Sunday fulfills the Sabbath: Christians keep the Lord's Day by Mass and rest as a precept of the Church, while the Sabbath's spiritual meaning is fulfilled in Christ (Catechism 2175–2176, 2180).

No law binds Christians to a particular day; the Third Commandment is kept by hearing God's word, and Sunday is kept for good order and worship (Large Catechism, Third Commandment). The rest of Hebrews 4 is rest in Christ.

settings.by: A leader of worship, or the congregation calling to itself ("Come, let us")
settings.when: At a festival procession into the temple, perhaps the autumn feast
settings.why: To gather the people in praise of the King and Creator, and to bring them to their knees before the God who made them and shepherds them.
settings.readers: Israel after the exile, gathered again at the rebuilt temple, sang it as the people of his pasture.

settings.what: A warning in God's own voice
settings.by: God, through a priest or prophet ("I," "me")
settings.to: The congregation, addressed as "you," the heirs of the wilderness generation
settings.when: In the same service, as the people enter
settings.why: To make sure that worship does not become empty: the people who sing must also listen, unlike their ancestors who saw God's works and still put him on trial.
settings.readers: For Jews after the exile, who had lost and regained the land, the oath that the wilderness generation would not enter God's rest was a sharp warning. Hebrews applied it to Christians tempted to drift away.
views: A prophetic sermon joined to a hymn

title: A New Song for All the Earth
sum: Psalm 96 calls all the earth to sing a new song to the LORD and the nations to hear the good news of his saving help. The gods of the peoples are nothing-gods; the LORD made the heavens. The clans of the peoples are to bring him glory and tribute, come into his courts, and bow low in holy splendor.

The message to the nations is "The LORD is King!" Because he reigns, the world stands firm, and he will govern the peoples with fairness. So heaven, earth, sea, fields and forests are to shout for joy, because he is coming to judge the world in the right way. Almost the whole psalm appears in 1 Chronicles 16:23–33. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 95.
readings: Read as a mission psalm
Israel is sent to tell the nations about the LORD; the nations are invited into his temple.
Read beside Isaiah 40–55
Good news, idols as nothing, the islands and nations, the coming of the LORD: many scholars hear Isaiah's voice and the return from exile.
Read as the coming judgment
Jews pray for the coming kingdom; Christians hear the return of Christ as judge.

views.H: The Hebrew has no title. The Greek reads "When the house was being built after the captivity. A song of David." Chronicles places the song at David's bringing of the ark to Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 16:7).
views.C: Most scholars think Chronicles quotes the psalm, adapted for a time before the temple ("his place" for "his sanctuary"). They date the psalm after the exile, from its closeness to Isaiah 40–55.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 95. In the synagogue it is part of Kabbalat Shabbat. In the Western church it is sung at Christmas Midnight Mass ("Let the heavens be glad"), and the Roman liturgy uses "The Lord has reigned" for Christ the King.
views.J: Jewish readers hear the psalm of the world to come, when all nations will know the LORD. Chronicles' setting made it part of David's song at the ark.
views.X: Justin Martyr and Tertullian quoted 96:10 as "The Lord has reigned from the tree," a reading of some Greek and Latin copies, and read it of the cross (see the variant). Paul's speech at Athens echoes 96:13 (Acts 17:31).

deep.h: "The Lord has reigned from the tree"
deep.b:
Around AD 155 Justin Martyr accused the Jewish teachers of his day of cutting words out of the Scriptures. One of his examples was Psalm 96:10, which he quoted as "Say among the nations, the Lord has reigned from the tree" (apo tou xylou), adding that the Jews had removed "from the tree" (Dialogue with Trypho 73). Tertullian, about fifty years later, quoted the same words twice. In the Latin West the reading Dominus regnavit a ligno spread through the Old Latin psalters, and Venantius Fortunatus' hymn Vexilla regis (AD 569) celebrates it: what David sang in faithful song is fulfilled, "God has reigned from the tree."

The evidence points the other way from Justin's charge. No Hebrew manuscript has the words. The great Greek manuscripts (Vaticanus, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus) lack them; Origen and Jerome knew no such Greek text; and 1 Chronicles 16:31 has the line without them. The words stand in the first hand of the Verona Psalter, a Greek and Latin manuscript of the 500s or 600s, where a later hand disapproved them (Swete's apparatus); Eberhard Nestle also reported them in the Greek minuscule 156 and the Sahidic Coptic version. Most scholars therefore think "from the tree" began as a Christian comment written beside the line and then entered some copies. It is a witness to how early Christians read the psalm: the King who reigns over the nations is Christ crucified. The Plain follows the Hebrew.
deep.refs: 96:10; 1 Chronicles 16:31; Galatians 3:13; Acts 5:30; Acts 10:39; 1 Peter 2:24; John 12:32

deep.b: The Plain of Psalm 96 uses the site's Plain of 1 Chronicles 16:23–33 wherever the Hebrew is the same. Where it differs: Chronicles leaves out 96:1a ("Sing a new song to the LORD") and 96:2a; it reads "strength and joy are in his place" for "strength and beauty" in "his sanctuary" (96:6; 1 Chronicles 16:27); "come into his presence" for "come into his courts" (96:8; 1 Chronicles 16:29); it has no "He will govern the peoples with fairness" (96:10c); it puts "may the nations be told, 'The LORD is King!'" after the heavens' gladness (1 Chronicles 16:31), not before it as in 96:10; it says "the open country" with a slightly different word; it has "he is coming" once (96:13 has it twice); and it ends before the last two lines of 96:13. Chronicles also continues with Psalm 106:1 and 106:47–48.

echoes: 1 Chronicles 16:23–33; Isaiah 40:9; Isaiah 42:10; Isaiah 52:7; Isaiah 44:23; Psalm 9:8; Psalm 29:1–2; Psalm 98:7–9; Acts 17:31; Revelation 5:9; Revelation 14:6–7; 1 Corinthians 10:20

settings.what: A hymn calling all nations to praise the King
settings.by: A temple singer, calling Israel and the nations
settings.to: Israel ("Sing," "bring the good news"), the nations and clans of the peoples (96:7–9), and all creation (96:11–12)
settings.when: In temple worship; Chronicles sets it at David's bringing of the ark to Jerusalem, the Greek title at the rebuilding of the temple after the exile.
settings.why: To proclaim to every nation that the LORD alone is God and King, that the idols are nothing, and that he is coming to set the world right. For Israel, a small people among empires, it turned faith into mission.
settings.readers: For Jews in the Persian and Greek worlds, surrounded by temples of other gods, it was both a confession and an invitation to the nations.
views: After the exile, at the rebuilding of the temple
The Greek title and most scholars.

title: Cloud and Fire Around the King
sum: "The LORD is King!" begins Psalm 97, and the earth and the far islands are glad. The King appears as at Sinai: cloud and thick darkness around him, fire going ahead to burn his foes, lightning that makes the earth writhe, mountains melting like wax. Yet his throne rests on righteousness and justice.

Those who worship carved images and boast of nothing-gods are put to shame, and the gods themselves must bow down. Zion hears and is glad. Those who love the LORD are told to hate evil; he guards his loyal ones, and light is sown for the righteous like seed for a harvest of joy. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 96.
readings: Read as a theophany
The psalm describes God's coming in storm and fire, using the language of Sinai and of the prophets' Day of the LORD.
Read as the defeat of idols
The King's appearing shames idol worshipers and humbles every god.
Read as comfort for the faithful
The fire that burns his foes is light and joy for the righteous (97:10–12).

views.H: The Hebrew has no title; the Greek reads "Of David, when his land is being restored." Rabbinic tradition counted it among Moses' psalms.
views.C: Scholars note how much of the psalm is made of older phrases: Sinai (Exodus 19–20), Psalm 18, Psalm 50, Micah 1, Psalm 48:11, Psalm 89:14. Many date it after the exile as a learned anthology of theophany language.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 96. In the synagogue it is part of Kabbalat Shabbat; 97:11 opens the Kol Nidre service in the Ashkenazi rite. In the Western church it is sung at the Christmas Mass at dawn ("A light will shine on us today").
views.J: The Targum reads 97:11 as "light stored up for the righteous," the hidden light of creation saved for the world to come (Bavli Chagigah 12a).
views.X: Hebrews 1:6 quotes "let all God's angels bow down to him," words close to the Greek of 97:7 and of Deuteronomy 32:43, and applies them to Christ. The church has sung the psalm of Christ's appearing at Christmas and of his return.

echoes: Exodus 19:16–18; Exodus 20:21; Deuteronomy 4:11; Deuteronomy 32:43; Psalm 18:7–15; Psalm 50:3; Psalm 89:14; Micah 1:3–4; Psalm 48:11; Isaiah 42:17; Hebrews 1:6; Amos 5:15

settings.what: A hymn of the King's appearing
settings.to: The worshipers and the whole earth (97:1–7), then the LORD (97:8–9), then the faithful (97:10–12)
settings.when: In temple worship, probably at a festival celebrating God's kingship; most scholars think after the exile.
settings.why: To celebrate God's rule as a powerful appearing that shames idols and gods, and to assure the faithful that the same power guards them and will bring them light and joy.
settings.readers: For Jews living among idol temples in the Persian and Greek world, the psalm's mockery of carved images and its promise of light were encouragement to stay faithful.

title: The Victory of the King
sum: Psalm 98 is the twin of Psalm 96. It too begins "Sing a new song to the LORD," but its reason is a victory already won: the LORD's right hand and holy arm brought him victory, he has made his saving help known before the nations, and he has remembered his loyal love to Israel, so that the far ends of the earth have seen how God saves.

So all the earth is to shout, sing and make music, with lyre, trumpets and ram's horn before the King. The sea, the world, the rivers and the mountains join in, clapping and ringing out with joy, because the LORD is coming to judge the world in the right way. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 97.
readings: Read as a victory song
Like the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15), it celebrates a rescue won by God alone: the exodus, the return from exile, or any deliverance.
Read as Isaiah's good news
Its words come close to Isaiah 52:7–10: the holy arm bared, the ends of the earth seeing God's salvation.
Read as a song of Christ's coming
Christians sing it at Christmas and of the return of Christ, most famously as "Joy to the World."

views.H: The Hebrew title is only "A psalm"; the Greek adds "of David," and the Targum calls it "a song of prophecy." Rabbinic tradition counted it among Moses' psalms.
views.C: Scholars note its close ties to Isaiah 40–55 (Isaiah 52:10; 59:16; 63:5) and to Psalm 96, and many date it after the exile. Its trumpets and ram's horn suggest a festival.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 97. In the synagogue it is part of Kabbalat Shabbat. In the Book of Common Prayer it is the Cantate Domino at Evening Prayer; the Roman liturgy sings it at Christmas ("All the ends of the earth have seen the saving power of God"). Isaac Watts' "Joy to the World" paraphrases 98:4–9.
views.J: The Targum's "song of prophecy" reads the victory as a future redemption. Jewish readers hear the coming kingdom when the LORD judges the world.
views.X: Mary's Magnificat echoes 98:1–3 (Luke 1:51–55), and Simeon's song speaks of seeing God's salvation prepared before all peoples (Luke 2:30–31). The church has read the psalm as fulfilled in Christ's coming.

echoes: Exodus 15:1–18; Isaiah 52:7–10; Isaiah 59:16; Isaiah 63:5; Isaiah 55:12; Psalm 96:1–13; Psalm 47:1–9; Luke 1:51–55; Luke 2:30–32; Romans 1:16–17

settings.what: A hymn celebrating the King's victory
settings.to: Israel and all the earth (98:1, 4), the musicians (98:5–6), and all creation (98:7–8)
settings.when: At a temple festival with trumpets and ram's horn; the victory itself is not named.
settings.why: To celebrate God's saving act as something done for Israel and seen by the whole world, and to call all creation to welcome the King who comes to judge.
settings.readers: For Jews after the return from Babylon, it read as the fulfillment of Isaiah's promise that the ends of the earth would see God's salvation.

title: Holy Is He
sum: The last of the psalms that open "The LORD is King!" Psalm 99 pictures the King seated on the cherubim in Zion, and calls the peoples to tremble and the earth to shake. Three times it ends a section with God's holiness: "Holy is he!" (99:3, 5) and "holy is the LORD our God" (99:9).

The King loves justice and has done justice in Jacob. The people are to bow at his footstool, the ark. The psalm remembers Moses, Aaron and Samuel, who called on God and were answered, who heard him from the pillar of cloud and kept his decrees. God forgave them and yet punished their wrongs. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 98.
readings: Read as a hymn of holiness
The threefold refrain makes holiness the theme: God's greatness (99:1–3), his justice (99:4–5), his forgiving and punishing (99:6–9).
Read as a temple psalm
Cherubim, footstool and holy mountain place the King in the Jerusalem temple.
Read as Israel's history in brief
Moses, Aaron and Samuel stand for the whole story of a people who prayed and were answered.

views.H: The Hebrew has no title; the Greek reads "A psalm of David." Rabbinic tradition counted it among Moses' psalms, which fits its naming of Moses.
views.C: Scholars compare its three-part holiness refrain with Isaiah 6:3 and date it variously, from the monarchy (because of the ark) to after the exile. They note how Book IV returns to Moses here (99:6) after Psalm 90.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 98. In the synagogue it is part of Kabbalat Shabbat, and 99:5 and 99:9 are sung when the Torah is taken out.
views.J: Rashi on 99:8 reads it as God forgiving Israel for these leaders' sake while punishing the leaders' own misdeeds: Moses and Aaron at Meribah, Samuel's failure with his sons. Radak hears 99:2 of the return of the Presence to Zion.
views.X: Christian readers have heard the threefold holy as an echo of the Trinity, and the priests and intercessors of 99:6 as pointing to Christ's priesthood (Hebrews 7:25). Augustine read the "footstool" of 99:5 as Christ's flesh, adored before it is eaten (Expositions of the Psalms 98.9).

echoes: Exodus 25:22; 1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Samuel 6:2; Isaiah 6:3; 1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalm 132:7; Exodus 33:9; Numbers 12:5; Numbers 20:12; Exodus 34:6–7; Jeremiah 15:1; Revelation 4:8

settings.what: A hymn to the holy King of Zion
settings.by: A temple singer, speaking for the people ("our God")
settings.to: The peoples and the earth (99:1–3), the LORD (99:4, 8), and the worshipers in Zion (99:5, 9)
settings.when: In the temple, before the ark, perhaps at a festival of God's kingship
settings.why: To proclaim God's holiness in his greatness, justice and dealings with his people, and to call worshipers to bow before him as their ancestors' leaders did.
settings.readers: For Jews after the exile, when the ark itself was lost, the memory of Moses, Aaron and Samuel assured them that God still answered those who called on his name.

title: Through His Gates with Thanks
sum: Psalm 100 is short and bright: all the earth is called to raise a shout to the LORD, to serve him with joy and come before him with glad shouts. The reason: the LORD is God, he made us, and we belong to him, his people and the flock he pastures.

So the worshipers come through his gates and into his courts with thanks and praise, for the LORD is good, his loyal love is forever, and his faithfulness lasts from generation to generation. The psalm closes the group of kingship psalms (93–100) and is one of the most sung texts in the world. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 99.
readings: Read as a song for the thank offering
The title links it to the todah, the thanksgiving sacrifice eaten in the temple (Leviticus 7:12–15).
Read as an entrance song
Its movement is a procession: through the gates, into the courts.
Read as a call to the nations
"All the earth" is invited into Israel's confession: the LORD is God, and we are his.

views.H: The title is "A psalm for the thank offering" (or "for thanksgiving"), with no author. Rabbinic tradition counted it as the last of Moses' eleven psalms.
views.C: Scholars read it as a hymn for entering the temple, closing the collection of 93–100 by echoing 95:6–7 ("he made us," "the flock he pastures"). It is often dated after the exile.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 99. In the Ashkenazi synagogue it is said in the weekday morning service, but not on Sabbaths, festivals, the eve of Yom Kippur or during Passover; other rites differ. In the Book of Common Prayer it is the Jubilate Deo of Morning Prayer, and in metrical form it is "All People That on Earth Do Dwell," sung to the Old Hundredth.
views.J: The Midrash on Psalms says that in the time to come all offerings will cease except the thank offering, and all prayers except thanksgiving. Rashi and the Targum read "and his we are" in 100:3.
views.X: Protestant and Catholic hymnody has made Psalm 100 a hymn of the universal church. The KJV's "and not we ourselves" (100:3) was long read as a confession that human beings cannot make or save themselves.

echoes: Leviticus 7:12–15; Psalm 95:6–7; Deuteronomy 4:39; 1 Kings 18:39; Psalm 118:19–20; 1 Chronicles 16:34; Jeremiah 33:11; Exodus 4:23; John 10:14–16

settings.what: A hymn for entering the temple with thanks
settings.by: A temple singer or leader of worship
settings.to: All the earth, and the worshipers coming to the temple
settings.when: As worshipers entered the temple courts, perhaps with the thank offering (the title)
settings.why: To invite everyone into joyful service of the LORD, grounded in the confession that he made us and owns us, and in his lasting goodness and loyal love.
settings.readers: For the community of the rebuilt temple, small among the nations, the call to "all the earth" carried the hope that the nations would one day enter too (Isaiah 56:7).

title: The King's Promise
sum: After the psalms of the LORD's kingship comes a human king's vow. "Of David," it begins: the king will sing of loyal love and justice and pledge himself to the blameless way, starting inside his own house. He will set nothing worthless before his eyes and keep crooked hearts and evil far away. In the middle he asks, "When will you come to me?"

He promises to silence secret slanderers, to have no patience with the proud, to choose the faithful of the land as his servants, and to let no liar or deceiver stay in his house. Every morning he will deal with the wicked, to rid the LORD's city of wrongdoers. In Greek and Latin Bibles it is Psalm 100.
readings: Read as a royal vow
A king of Judah pledges at his crowning, or at a yearly festival, to rule justly, as Deuteronomy 17:18–20 requires.
Read as a mirror for rulers
Luther and many after him read it as a pattern for every Christian ruler and official.
Read as a personal vow
Many readers take it as anyone's resolve to keep heart and home clean before God.

views.H: The title gives it to David. Traditional readers place it early in his reign, perhaps while he waited for the ark to come to Jerusalem (101:2; 2 Samuel 6:9).
views.C: Most scholars class it as a royal psalm from the monarchy, a king's oath at his enthronement. Its placement after Psalms 93–100 makes the human king answer to the divine King.
views.L: Greek and Latin numbering: Psalm 100. It has been used at the installation of rulers and magistrates in Protestant lands, and in monastic tradition as a psalm of self-examination.
views.J: Rashi and the Targum read 101:1 as praising God for both kindness and judgment (compare Bavli Berakhot 60b). The Targum reads "my house" in 101:2 as "my house of study."
views.X: Augustine heard Christ, the just King, speaking. Luther's exposition (1534), written for Elector John Frederick of Saxony, treats it as a handbook of good government and a warning against flatterers at court.

echoes: Deuteronomy 17:18–20; 2 Samuel 6:9; 2 Samuel 23:3–4; Psalm 15:1–5; Psalm 24:3–4; Proverbs 20:8; Proverbs 25:5; Proverbs 29:12; Isaiah 11:3–5; Jeremiah 21:12

settings.by: The king ("Of David"), speaking in the first person
settings.to: The LORD (101:1–2) and, by implication, his court and people
settings.when: Perhaps at the king's coronation or at a yearly renewal of the covenant between king and God
settings.why: To bind the king publicly to loyal love and justice, beginning with his own conduct and household, and to promise protection for the faithful and an end to corruption.
settings.readers: After the exile, with no king, the psalm kept alive the picture of the king Israel hoped for, and it taught every reader to measure leaders by it.
views: Some scholars and many devotional readers.
